clue.text: Francois points out the Sea to a Florentine

parts.note: the Med is the usual short name for the Mediterranean Sea
a Frenchman pointing something out says 'ici', French for 'here'

explanation.surface: A Frenchman shows an Italian visitor the view of the Mediterranean.
explanation.walkthrough: François stands for any Frenchman, and what he says when pointing is ICI ('here'). The pieces come in answer order: MED first, then ICI.
explanation.definitionFit: The Medici were the banking dynasty who ruled Florence, so a member of the family is a Florentine.

clue.text: Club-speed appears steep.

parts.note: a mace is a heavy club
rate means speed

explanation.surface: How fast a golf club swings looks steep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'appears' only links; 'steep' is the verb, to soak.
explanation.definitionFit: To macerate is to soften something by soaking it in liquid.

clue.text: Reduced to the ranks for a witticism indeed!

indicators.note: the word indeed splits as in plus deed, so the in places the witticism inside

parts.note: taken as written, the second half of indeed
a mot is a witty saying, as in bon mot

explanation.surface: A soldier is busted down for cracking a joke.
explanation.walkthrough: The device is to read 'indeed' as two words, 'in deed', so the 'in' tells you where the witticism goes. A bon mot is a clever remark.
explanation.definitionFit: A soldier demoted is reduced in rank, sent back to the ranks as a private.

clue.text: Singer is against taking a lot of trouble

parts.note: contra means against

indicators.note: lot in a state of trouble means its letters are disturbed

explanation.surface: A singer is opposed to going to great effort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a lot of trouble' looks like great effort, but 'of trouble' is the anagram signal working on 'lot', and 'taking' only joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A contralto is a low female voice, and a woman who sings with it.

clue.text: Oddly enough DOM plays music in church

indicators.note: something done oddly is done out of order, so the letters that follow are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written; Dom is also the title of a Benedictine monk

explanation.surface: A monk, surprisingly, turns out to be the one performing the music in church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly enough' rearranges DOM and PLAYS together; 'plays' looks like the verb of the sentence but is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Psalmody is the singing of psalms, a kind of sacred music used in services.

clue.text: Dickensian Hampstead Ponds speculator

parts.note: the founder of the club in Dickens's first novel wrote a paper speculating on the source of the Hampstead Ponds

explanation.surface: A character from Dickens who theorised about some London ponds.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Pickwick Papers the hero's paper is 'Speculations on the Source of the Hampstead Ponds'; Hampstead is a district of London.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of The Pickwick Papers is the gentleman who wrote those speculations.

clue.text: Theatre of song

definitions.meaning: a well-known theatre in London's West End
as an adjective it means relating to songs or singing

explanation.walkthrough: The Lyric is a theatre on Shaftesbury Avenue in London.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lyric Theatre is a London playhouse, and the adjective describes poetry meant to be sung.

clue.text: Prevent complications above it

indicators.note: complications tangle the letters of the words that follow into a new order

explanation.surface: Avoiding trouble higher up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'complications' looks like what is prevented, but it shuffles ABOVE IT.
explanation.definitionFit: To obviate a problem is to remove it in advance, so it never happens.

clue.text: There's the Yorkist leader taking on red uprising

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter
in a down clue an uprising reads the word from the bottom up, backwards

explanation.surface: A Yorkist commander takes on the rising of Lancastrian reds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking' joins Y to ON; 'uprising' reverses RED to DER in this down clue. The definition 'There's' stands for 'There is', i.e. over there.
explanation.definitionFit: Yonder means over there, at a distance, pointing to a place.

clue.text: Bobby went to Davy Jones's locker, though the ship was so sound ?

parts.note: a bobby is a British policeman, and so is a copper
Davy Jones's locker is the sea bed, so going there is hitting bottom

explanation.surface: A policeman drowned at sea, though the vessel was seaworthy.
explanation.walkthrough: Bobby and copper are both British slang for a policeman. Ships were sheathed in copper below the waterline, which is why the word came to mean thoroughly sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Something copper-bottomed is reliable and safe, like a ship whose hull is sheathed against rot.

clue.text: Red organization took care of many in class

parts.note: c/o, the postal abbreviation for 'care of'
M, the Roman numeral for a thousand, is a crossword stand-in for many
a form is a school class

explanation.surface: A left-wing body looked after a lot of people in a schoolroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'took' only joins definition to wordplay. A form is a class in a British school.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cominform was the Communist Information Bureau set up by Moscow in 1947, a Communist body.

clue.text: Nothing outlandish about a number being split

indicators.note: about means going round, so the first piece wraps the second

parts.note: a foreign word for nothing: French 'rien'
V is the Roman numeral five

explanation.surface: Something about a figure being divided is not unusual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outlandish' means foreign here, asking for a foreign word for 'nothing'; 'about' puts V (five) inside RIEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Riven is the old past participle of rive, to tear apart, so it means torn or cleft.

clue.text: Role Jack sent back that of grain store protector

indicators.note: sending something back here reads the whole run of letters in reverse order

parts.note: an actor's part is a role
a jack tar is a sailor, so Jack gives tar

explanation.surface: An actor's role is returned, the one guarding the granary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sent back' turns PART + TAR into RAT TRAP. A jack tar is an old name for a sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: A trap for rats is a device to keep vermin out of stored grain.

clue.text: Set a gem, engrave the metal -points to pursue

definitions.text: Set a gem, engrave the metal

parts.note: E and N are two compass points, east and north
to chase is to pursue

explanation.surface: A jeweller's instructions: set the stone, cut the metal, chase the details.
explanation.walkthrough: The long definition gives two senses of the verb, setting a jewel and engraving metal. 'points' are compass points.
explanation.definitionFit: To enchase is to set a jewel in an ornamental mount, and also to engrave or emboss metalwork.

clue.text: This river goes both ways from time to time

definitions.text: This river goes both ways from time to time

parts.words: This river goes both ways from time to time
parts.note: a river near the sea that flows inland and back out again as the sea rises and falls

explanation.surface: A river that changes direction now and then.
explanation.definitionFit: Near the coast a river's current reverses with the rise and fall of the sea twice a day.

clue.text: News-hound about to take a drink

parts.note: re means about or concerning
porter is a dark beer

explanation.surface: A journalist is about to go for a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about to' looks like 'on the point of', but 'about' is RE and 'to take' joins it to PORTER, a dark beer.
explanation.definitionFit: News-hound is slang for a journalist who chases stories.

clue.text: Turn-out altered morale ? What rambling talk !

parts.note: a rig or rig-out is an outfit, a turn-out

indicators.note: altered says the letters of morale are changed into another order

explanation.surface: A parade's changed spirits get a long-winded speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn-out' means an outfit here, not a crowd or a result, and 'altered' is the anagram signal working on 'morale'.
explanation.definitionFit: A rigmarole is a long, confused story or a tedious procedure.

clue.text: How pupils so placed in class came pouring out.?

definitions.meaning: pupils sorted into classes by ability are placed in sets or bands
flowed out in a steady current

explanation.walkthrough: British schools 'stream' pupils by putting them in classes by ability.
explanation.definitionFit: Schools group children by ability into ranked groups, and the verb also means flowed copiously.

clue.text: Living in the Middle Ages geologically ?

definitions.text: Living in the Middle Ages geologically ?

parts.words: Living in the Middle Ages geologically
parts.note: the geological era whose name means 'middle life', between the Palaeozoic and the Cenozoic

explanation.surface: Someone stuck in medieval times, in rock terms.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mesozoic era, the age of dinosaurs, takes its name from Greek for middle and life.

clue.text: The amendment I state is right and proper

indicators.note: an amendment changes the word the, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: Cal is an abbreviation for California, a US state

explanation.surface: A legislator states that a change to the law is fair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'amendment' rearranges THE to ETH, then I and CAL (California).
explanation.definitionFit: Ethical conduct is morally sound and fitting.

clue.text: Some are born so, Malvolio read

definitions.text: Some are born so, Malvolio read

parts.words: Some are born so, Malvolio read
parts.note: in Twelfth Night Malvolio reads a forged letter: 'Some are born ..., some achieve ..., and some have ... thrust upon them'

explanation.surface: A line from the letter read aloud by Malvolio in Shakespeare's play.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue quotes the forged letter in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night, which Malvolio reads; the missing word is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: The quotation's missing adjective, meaning eminent or illustrious, completes the famous line.

clue.text: Absorb two points over the twelve dozen

indicators.note: in a down clue over places the first piece above the second

parts.note: E and N are two compass points
a gross is twelve dozen, 144

explanation.surface: Two marks scored on top of a gross of something.
explanation.definitionFit: To engross is to occupy someone's attention completely.

clue.text: Rainbow girl raised American dog star

indicators.note: raised in a down clue lifts the letters so they read upwards, backwards

parts.note: Iris is the Greek goddess of the rainbow

explanation.surface: A girl named Rainbow brings up an American celebrity dog.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth Iris is the goddess of the rainbow, and 'raised' reads her name upwards in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Sirius, in Canis Major, is called the Dog Star.

clue.text: What to do to a house, one in Bath perhaps ?

definitions.text: What to do to a house

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: perhaps signals the letters might be arranged some other way

explanation.surface: Advice on a house, perhaps a home in the city of Bath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' shuffles I (one) with IN and BATH; Bath, a spa city in England, looks like the place to live.
explanation.definitionFit: To inhabit a house is to live in it, the thing a house is for.

clue.text: With such pals cleavage means sticking together?

definitions.text: With such pals cleavage means sticking together?

parts.words: With such pals cleavage means sticking together
parts.note: close friends are called by the word for the chest, and a cleavage is literally a parting yet here sits between the two halves of the chest

explanation.surface: A remark that friends who split up still stick together.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for close friends ('... pals') is also the chest, where a cleavage lies, so a splitting word becomes a sign of closeness.
explanation.definitionFit: Bosom pals are intimate friends, and the cleavage is the hollow of the chest.

clue.text: Argue as mathematicians?

parts.note: at Cambridge a student with a first in mathematics is called a ..., so the verb for arguing doubles as what such scholars do

explanation.surface: A row among maths students.
explanation.walkthrough: At Cambridge University a first-class mathematics graduate is called a Wrangler.
explanation.definitionFit: To dispute noisily is to bicker or argue, and the Cambridge title for top maths graduates comes from it.

clue.text: Old S American dynasty in and about the South

parts.note: ca, short for circa, means about
S is the abbreviation for south

explanation.surface: Notes on an ancient South American ruling family located in the south.
explanation.definitionFit: The Inca emperors ruled Peru and the Andes before the Spanish conquest.

clue.text: Everything's so big !

parts.note: the whole universe seen as one vast system, the opposite of the tiny world of man

explanation.surface: An exclamation at how large it all is.
explanation.definitionFit: The macrocosm is the universe as a whole, the greatest of all structures.

clue.text: Did this man usurp God's creative function?

definitions.text: Did this man usurp God's creative function?

parts.words: Did this man usurp God's creative function
parts.note: a man said to have created himself, as if taking God's job of making people

explanation.surface: A question about a man who played God by making himself.
explanation.walkthrough: A man who rose by his own efforts is said to have made himself, which reads literally as taking over creation.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who achieves success unaided is called this, having built his own fortune.

clue.text: "Few could know When Lucy to be '" (Wordsworth)

definitions.text: "Few could know When Lucy to be '" (Wordsworth)

parts.words: "Few could know When Lucy to be '" (Wordsworth)
parts.note: Wordsworth's poem 'She dwelt among the untrodden ways' says few could know when Lucy stopped living

explanation.surface: A line from Wordsworth's Lucy poems with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap in the quotation from Wordsworth's 'She dwelt among the untrodden ways' takes a verb meaning stopped.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means stopped or came to an end, here of Lucy's life.
